options.label: Low / titrating
options.note: Below or early in dose titration — sub-maximal receptor engagement.

options.label: Therapeutic
options.note: Therapeutic-equivalent maintenance exposure.

options.label: High / experimental
options.note: Supra-therapeutic or experimental dosing — the dose-limiting side effects appear here.

options.label: Peripheral · therapeutic
options.note: Peripheral injection at a therapeutic dose — the marketed-drug route.

options.label: Peripheral · experimental
options.note: Peripheral but at experimental doses — common in rodent pharmacology.

options.label: Central · ICV
options.note: Intracerebroventricular — brain concentrations no peripheral dose reaches.

options.label: Central · intraparenchymal
options.note: Direct microinjection into a region — establishes that a node can produce an effect.

options.label: Acute
options.note: Single or short exposure — captures the spiky transient, not the adapted state.

options.label: Subacute
options.note: Days to weeks — partial adaptation underway.

options.label: Chronic
options.note: Sustained dosing — desensitisation and metabolic improvement reshape the picture.

options.label: Human
options.note: The translational target — but most mechanistic detail is inferred here, not measured.

options.label: Non-human primate
options.note: Amygdalar GLP-1R denser than rodent; the closest model to human affective circuitry.

options.label: Rat
options.note: Much of the circuit work — but receptor distribution differs from primate.

options.label: Mouse
options.note: Where the genetic tools live; hippocampal expression differs even from rat.

options.label: Pooled / unreported
options.note: Sexes pooled — the default of most human pharmacology data.

options.label: Female
options.note: Greater central anorectic and motivational response in rodents; estrogen interacts.

options.label: Male
options.note: The default subject of most rodent work.

options.label: Obesity
options.note: The pivotal-trial population — more intake to suppress, metabolic gain lifts mood.

options.label: Lean / healthy
options.note: Lean and metabolically healthy — effects on cognition and reward here are essentially unstudied.

options.label: Substance use disorder
options.note: Comorbid substance use disorder — the cross-reward trial population.

options.label: Semaglutide
options.note: Potent, long-acting; the most-studied agonist across reward and metabolic endpoints.

options.label: Liraglutide
options.note: Daily, shorter-acting; large fMRI cue-reactivity and gastric-emptying literature.

options.label: Exendin-4
options.note: The experimental rodent tool — sharper aversive profile, rarely a clinical regime.

options.label: Tirzepatide
options.note: Dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist — metabolically potent, central effects barely characterised.

options.label: Native GLP-1
options.note: Endogenous, phasic, degraded within minutes — the signal the drugs mimic, not a drug regime.

presets.label: Clinical register
presets.note: Chronic peripheral semaglutide in adults with obesity — the regime the marketed-drug claims actually live in.

presets.label: The fragile paradigm
presets.note: Acute ICV exendin-4 in lean male rats — the rodent mechanistic paradigm. The PRD's warning, made into a setting you can flip to.

presets.label: Cross-reward trial
presets.note: Chronic peripheral semaglutide in adults with alcohol use disorder — the regime the addiction trials read out in.

openQuestions: Which patients fall in the dysphoria / anhedonia tail — and is the moderator that predicts them dose, titration speed, baseline reward sensitivity, or a GLP-1R variant?
Sex-stratified human pharmacology is largely absent. Do the female-greater rodent anorectic and motivational effects hold in humans?
How does the system respond to chronic agonism — desensitisation, receptor trafficking, compensatory plasticity — and over what timescale?
Do GIP/GLP-1 dual and triple agonists share the central moderator profile of the single agonists, or is their brain pharmacology different in kind?
